title: 13 Things Schools and States Can Do to Protect Children from EdTech Harms
author: Emily Cherkin
summary: Emily Cherkin shares the solutions section of her October 2026 testimony to the Kentucky Budget Review Subcommittee on Education, now expanded to thirteen recommendations for lawmakers. She opens with four questions any child-facing technology must answer yes to, namely whether it is effective, safe, legal and superior to a human educator, and says the current answer to all four is no. Her recommendations include a comprehensive EdTech audit, ending 1:1 devices, prioritizing paper curricula and tests, a public registry and allow list of vetted products, informed parental consent, and a pause on generative AI products for children. She explains how vendor pricing creeps up once districts are dependent, and warns that Google is shifting legal liability onto districts. She closes with her tech-intentional stance that the best preparation for a digital future is an analog childhood and classroom.
points: Cherkin's gatekeeping test asks four yes-or-no questions before any device or product reaches children: effective, safe, legal, and superior to a human educator.
She recommends auditing every EdTech contract and pausing new adoptions, noting that districts average hundreds or thousands of unvetted products per school.
Her structural fixes favor paper textbooks, paper tests and report cards, computer labs instead of 1:1 devices, and an allow list instead of an endless block list.
She rejects screen-time limits as a solution because they ignore data privacy, harmful content and the displacement of human teachers.
She warns that the EdTech business model of cheap entry followed by rising renewals, plus shifting legal liability onto districts, makes continued dependence a financial and legal risk.
quotes: Currently, the answer to all four of these questions is a resounding NO and lawmakers must resist pressure to move forward on or further deploy any EdTech product use until we get to four YESes.
Remove 1:1 digital devices for PreK-12th grade students. This does not mean eliminating technology.
Many schools have moved away from paper and physical texts, in spite of decades of evidence that children learn better on paper and pencil.
The testing industry benefits when children test more; children do not benefit.
Just like Big Tech, EdTech vendors cannot and should not be trusted to regulate themselves.

Do not rely on “time limits” as a solution. While I applaud any efforts to roll back screen use, cutting time alone does not address the data privacy risks, exposure to problematic content, or the fact that what’s being done on the screen very well could be displacing an interaction with a human teacher.

they offer districts free or low-cost versions of their products, get a school or group of teachers dependent on it, then charge more in subsequent years, once the district and teachers and students are deeply enmeshed.
Children are not “scalable” or “standardized.” Education isn’t– or shouldn’t be– predicated on a financial “return on investment.
The best preparation we can offer our children for a digital future is an analog childhood and an analog classroom.
